title: Valid Anagram
keyIdea: Anagrams have the same letter counts. Keep one counter per letter: +1 for each letter of s, −1 for each letter of t. If every counter ends at 0, the letters cancel exactly and it's an anagram.

approaches.name: Sort both
approaches.idea: Sort both strings. Anagrams turn into the exact same string, so just compare them.
approaches.why: Two sorts of n characters each, then an O(n) comparison. Sorting is in place, so no extra container (std::sort uses O(log n) stack). s and t are passed by value, so the caller's strings stay untouched.

approaches.name: Hash map counts
approaches.idea: Count each character of s in an unordered_map, then subtract for each character of t. If a count ever drops below 0, t has a letter s doesn't have enough of.
approaches.why: One pass over each string, O(1) average per map update. k is the number of different characters. This is the answer to the Unicode follow-up.

approaches.name: Count array of 26
approaches.idea: freq[26], one slot per letter. In one loop: freq[s[i]-'a']++ and freq[t[i]-'a']--. Then every slot must be 0.
approaches.why: One pass over the strings plus a fixed 26 checks. The array is always 26 ints no matter how long the strings are, so the space is constant.

options: The ASCII code of the letter
The position of the letter in s

quiz.q: After the loop, freq['c'] = −1. What does that mean?
options: t has one more 'c' than s
s has one more 'c' than t

quiz.q: Why is the space O(1) even though we use an array?
options: It's always 26 ints, whatever the string length
Because we only use one loop

quiz.q: Follow-up: the strings can contain any Unicode characters. What do you change?
options: Use an unordered_map<char/int, int> instead of freq[26]
